The aim of this agreement is to standardize, for NATO forces, a method of computing the Military Load Classification (MLC in the text) of: a. All bridges and military ferries and rafts (including their landing stages), b. Military vehicles
A secondary objective is to e nhance interoperability of forces working in the same area.
Finally, selected parts of this agreement may also be used as a basis for the design of military equipment.

Participating nations agree that NATO forces will use the military load classification method given below. Partner Nations (PfP) and Mediterranean Dialogue (MD) Nations are encouraged to use the military load classification method given below as a way of extending standardization and facilitating the safe use of bridges worldwide. The conditions and standards of military load classification given in this agreement are not intended to govern existing or future civil bridge design or construction.
The latest version of this agreement with all the associated documents and software can be downloaded free of charges by the NATO forces and other partner nations. POC: MILENG CoE www.milengcoe.org.

The procedure detailed below gives a standard method of enabling all bridges, military ferries and rafts (including their landing stages) and military laden vehicles to be allocated an MLC number indicating the relationship between the load carrying capacity of the former and the loading effect produced by the latter. THE MILITARY LOAD CLASSIFICATION NUMBER IS ONLY A NUMBER, IT DOES NOT REPRESENT THE MASS OF THE VEHICLE.

If the nominal vehicle MLC is less than or equal to the MLC of the bridge (MLCvehicle ≤ MLCbridge), ferry or raft (and of its landing stage), the vehicle can cross the bridge or be embarked on the ferry or raft; otherwise, it must be diverted , unless span- and/or vehicle-specific analysis is conducted to provide a more accurate assessment of vehicle passability. If circumstances warrant, it may be possible for the vehicle to cross by implementing exceptional crossing conditions, as outlined in Annex H.

Under exceptional operational conditions, this prohibition may be lifted on special decision of the th eatre commander in the operational zone, or on that of the civil authorities in areas under their control.

Crossing of bridges by extremely heavy vehicles (in excess of MLC 150) must be assessed on a case-by-case basis even if the inequality MLCvehicle ≤ MLCbridge is respected. It is particularly recommended to check whether the axles are designed to produce a lateral distribution of the loads equivalent to - or even better than - the hypothetical vehicles of similar longitudinal load effects. This case-by-case assessment is highly recommended for vehicles exceeding MLC 120.
The method of marking the appropriate MLC on bridges, ferries, rafts (including their landing stages) and vehicles is detailed in Annex J.

On campaign in an emergency situation, an additional quick and simple method is proposed for a temporary classification of the military or civil vehicles or combinations that have not yet been classified. Also, expedient methods are proposed for a temporary classification of civilian fixed bridges not yet classified.

Bridges are rated according to AEP -3.12.1.5 only for military traffic. In peace time or during peace support operations, simultaneous civilian traffic can be authorized . Where possible, such dual use of bridges should be approved through a bilateral agreement between civilian and military authorities.

Thirty-two hypothetical vehicles (16 tracked vehicles and 16 wheeled vehicles - with various axle and wheel configurations) are defined by their main characteristics in SI units (Annex A) and establish thirty-two standard classes betw een MLC 4 and MLC 150 inclusive. Additional characteristics (height of centre of gravity, side wind area and height of centre of pressure) are also defined but are required only for the classification of bridges, ferries and rafts.
The mass in "short tons" (907 kg) of each hypothetical tracked vehicle is chosen as the MLC, but the mass of the hypothetical wheeled vehicle is different from its MLC.

In addition, for each wheeled vehicle military load class, a maximum single axle load and a nominal ground cont act length , a tyre load and a nominal ground contact width, and an axle wheel spacing and a nominal ground contact width are specified.
Vehicular loadings are defined by the hypothetical vehicles in Annex A. Column # Item

Tracked vehicles must be treated as uniformly distributed loads over both tracks (pressure or line loads with fixed length). The choice of the model depends on the capabilities of the method used for the structural analysis. For the hypothetical vehicles, the dimensions of the tracks are given in column 2 in Annex A. The maximum local load applied by a tracked vehicle road wheel will also be checked against the maximum local load corresponding to half of the maximum single axle load (column 4 in Annex A). For the maximum ground pressure, it would be considered that each tracked vehicle road wheel presses on the bridge deck via the pad(s) of a tracked link.

Axles of wheeled vehicles m ay be considered as concentrated loads or uniformly distributed loads (pressure or line loads with fixed length). The choice of the model depends on the capabilities of the method used for the structural analysis. This uniform load would be applied over t he load distribution area developed for the tyre assuming a ground contact width and a ground contact length defined in Annex A for each load class. The point load would be applied at the centre of the load distribution area.

section: 2.3 LOAD EFFECTS GENERATED BY HYPOTHETICAL VEHICLES
text: As bending and shear are generally considered as the main failure mechanisms, the maximum bending moments and shear forces generated by either of the hypothetical vehicles or by the maximum single-axle load on simply supported spans from 1 m to 100 m have been calculated.

section: 2.3 LOAD EFFECTS GENERATED BY HYPOTHETICAL VEHICLES
text: In order to simplify subsequent plotting of the MLC curves, the bending moments are divided by the corresponding span and called «unit bending moments».

section: 2.3 LOAD EFFECTS GENERATED BY HYPOTHETICAL VEHICLES
text: The tables 1 through 4 in Annex B give these unit bending moments and shear forces in SI units for both tracked and wheeled hypothetical vehicles. The corresponding curves are plotted in Annex C.

section: 2.3 LOAD EFFECTS GENERATED BY HYPOTHETICAL VEHICLES
text: The corresponding calculations have been carried out: a. With no allowance for dynamic coefficients or vehicle eccentricity. b. On the assumption that the nearest ground contact points of vehicles wheeled or tracked - are 30.50 m1 apart2. c. Treating axles as concentrated loads.
The curves representing the unit bending moments and shear forces as a function of span have been plotted for each major MLC on spans from 1 m to 100 m, and are given in SI units in Annex C.
The MLC curves are plotted separately for wheeled and tracked vehicles.
These curves are used for the MLC of both vehicles and simply supported single-span bridges. They must be recalculated for all the other configurations of bridges, ferries and rafts.

When the effects of actual vehicles or the bridge strengths are compared to the effects of the sets of hypo thetical vehicles, the following interpolation/extrapolation rule is applicable: 1. If the resulting MLC lies between the curves of two successive hypothetical vehicles, a simple linear interpolation will be used. 2. If the resulting MLC is higher than 150, it will be designated MLC 150+. For a relative comparison of the load effects, the calculation will be carried out with a simple proportionality rule referring to the curve relative to the MLC 150 hypothetical vehicle. A detailed analysis procedure or the approach as outlined in Section 4.1.10 should be applied, as appropriate, when a bridge is crossed by an MLC 150+ vehicle. 3. If the resulting MLC is lower than 4, the calculation will be carried out with a simple proportionality rule referring to the curve relative to the MLC 4 hypothetical vehicle. 4. At the end of the calculations, the resulting MLC shall be rounded off to the nearest whole figure (e.g., calculated MLC 56.2 rounded off to MLC 56 or MLC 49.5 rounded off to MLC 50). 5. As the rating is based on the effects of the vehicles, there is no need to define "intermediate" hypothetical vehicles. Applying the present interpolation/extrapolation rule, it is possible to calculate the effects of "intermediate" vehicles as required.

Solo vehicles, the normal components of vehicle combinations3, and trailers are classified in their fully laden state - as defined hereafter - according to the procedures " 3.2" and " 3.3" defined below. For the others cases, see the procedure "3.4" defined below.

section: 3.1 CHARACTERISATION OF A VEHICLE IN FULLY LADEN STATE
text: The characteristics of a given vehicle in fully laden state must so be taken that its load effects will never be exceeded in normal operational use. They are fixed by the appropriate national authority (see annex F) with vehicle(s) loaded to the maximum allowed payload. Where possible, they are based on actual measured behaviour. Otherwise, the distribution of loads to the individual axles or tracks should be assigned in a rational manner considering the vehicle details and the anticipated payload. The way the vehicle's data has been determined should be included in the MLC vehicle databases described in Section 3.5.

section: 3.1 CHARACTERISATION OF A VEHICLE IN FULLY LADEN STATE
text: The characteristics of tracked vehicles should always be based on the full combat load for the configuration. Even if the position of its centre of gravity in running configuration is not fixed (due to the orientation of the turret for instance), it can well be assumed that its gross weight is uniformly distributed over the ground. The following data must be collected: • The maximum gross weight in operation, • The ground contact width (as defined in Annex D), • The dimensions of the footprint, assumed rectangular, namely the track length and the track width.

section: 3.1 CHARACTERISATION OF A VEHICLE IN FULLY LADEN STATE
text: Even at their maximum allowed payload, wheeled vehicles can present highly variable axle weights due to the variable position of the centre of gravity of the payload, depending on the way the vehicles are loaded. For this reason, it is not sufficient to only consider the maximum gross weight. For the MLC calculation of wheeled vehicles, the axle weights are relevant. The following data must be collected: • The maximum gross weight in operation, • The maximum expected axle weights, • The spacings between the successive axles, • The ground contact width (as defined in Annex D), • The dimensions of the footprints, assumed rectangular, ideally for all axles, otherwise for the heaviest axle(s).

section: 3.1 CHARACTERISATION OF A VEHICLE IN FULLY LADEN STATE
text: Wheeled vehicles can be separated into three categories:

section: 3.1 CHARACTERISATION OF A VEHICLE IN FULLY LADEN STATE
text: 3 e.g.: Prime mover and semi-trailer, e.g. tractor and gun

section: 3.1 CHARACTERISATION OF A VEHICLE IN FULLY LADEN STATE
text: • Armoured vehicles on wheels are comparable to tracked vehicles because they are generally compact. The sum of their maximum axle weights is practically equal to the maximum gross weight. • Fixed load vehicles with well-defined maximum payloads in running configuration present almost fixed centre of gravity so that the sum of their maximum axle weights is also practically equal to the maximum gross weight (examples: tank trucks, mobile cranes, fire vehicles). • Variable load vehicles that do not have clearly defined payload s - such as vehicles primarily used for general-purpose transportation - present highly variable axle weights even at maximum payload so that the sum of their maximum axle weights and their maximum gross weights may be significantly different.

section: 3.1 CHARACTERISATION OF A VEHICLE IN FULLY LADEN STATE
text: If it appears that the maximum gross weights or axle weights used for classification are exceeded in operation, the vehicle's MLC should be recalculated.

To classify a given sin gle vehicle or combination, it is necessary to calculate the maximum unit bending moments and shear forces which it produces on the various reference spans. The values so obtained are plotted over the MLC curves of Annex C.

The vehicle spacing of 30.5m as outlined in Section 2.3.4. is used when calculating forces for vehicle MLC rating . The span-dependent MLCs of the vehicle are determined by applying the interpolation/extrapolation outlined in Section 2.5. Wheeled vehicles will be classified using the curv es on Annex C (Figures 1 through 4). Tracked vehicles will be classified using the curves on Annex C (Figures 5 through 8).
The nominal MLC of vehicles is defined as the maximum value for all spans between 1 m and 100 m.

It is highly recommended to store the complete span-dependent MLC curves (calculated with and without the width correction for narrow vehicles), at least for the heaviest vehicles used in operation and for vehicles presenting MLC curves with a peak value at short spans. For these vehicles, it is also recommended to store the MLC curves for vehicles running one vehicle at a time. Only personnel sufficiently qualified in bridge assessment are allowed to use such span-dependent MLC curves. An MLC based on a single span or range of spans will only be used as a temporary MLC. The permanent MLC assigned to the vehicle will remain the highest MLC associated with all spans between 1 m and 100 m. Software supporting a span-dependent MLC are listed in Annexe F.

For vehicles narrower than the hypothetical vehicle, the interpolated MLC is adjusted for vehicle width effect. For vehicles wider than the hypothetical vehicle, no such adjustment is made. The total width across ground contact points of the widest axle of a wheeled vehicle or vehicle combination or of the tracks for a tracked vehicle to be classified is compared with that of the equivalent hypothetical vehicle having the same class. The latter width is obtained by linear interpolation between the ground contact widths of the standard hypothetical vehicles. The calculated difference in width must then be multiplied by the appropriate width correction factor as outlined in Annex D to determine the extent to which the interpolated MLC must be increased.

When the g round contact length of a single tyre of an axle is known, the axle load may be equated to a load evenly distributed over the ground contact length. In such cases, the tyre data given in Annex A, columns 4 to 6, are not to be taken into consideration.
Examples of calculation for determining the MLC of vehicles are given in Annex E.

Rapid and highly accurate results may be obtained by means of a computer, without the need for plotting the curves. In this case, it is recommended to use one of the reference software described in Annex F.

The reference software is the recommended means to calculate and determine, under the responsibility of the national official authorities, the permanent MLC of a vehicle (The particulars of the software national depository authorities are recorded in a separate database as outlined in Annex F).

On campaign in an emergency, the MLC of an unclassified vehicle or combination may be assessed easily and quickly, by factoring the equivalent total laden mass indicated on the manufacturer's plate or in the operating manual. This results in a temporary MLC which cannot be marked on the vehicle. This method also allows a temporary MLC to be allocated to an unladen vehicle or combination by factoring the equivalent unladen mass indicated on the manufacturer's plate or the operating manual.

For all vehicle types - tracked or wheeled - the temporary MLC will be calculated multiplying the total laden mass of the vehicle or combination by the following coefficient: • 1.25 if the total laden mass is expressed in metric Tonnes (t), • 1.14 if the total laden mass is expressed in short tons (st), • 0.57 if the total laden mass is expressed in kilo pounds (kip),
A pocket reminder is given in Annex G for the personnel in charge of crossing sites.
Examples of calculations used to determine the temporary MLC of vehicles are given in Annex G.
A vehicle may temporarily receive an MLC number in the unladen or partial load configuration.

For analytical rating, vehicle load combinations made up of their normal components receive an MLC for the whole train, laden or unladen as appropriate. For semi-trailers, the calculation is done with the normal distribution of weight transfer to the tractor's articulation point (i.e., fifth wheel). If both vehicles are wheeled or both are tracked, the combination vehicle MLC will be considered as a wheeled or tracked vehicle MLC respectively. The MLC of a combined vehicle formed from a tracked vehicle and a wheeled vehicle shall be calculated clearly stating which vehicle type (tracked or wheeled) is taken as reference.

As an expedient alternative for a vehicle train of two vehicles, one towing another not normally associated with it, the combined MLC should be calculated as follows: a. If the sum of the two vehicles' MLC is less than 60, the combined military load classification number of the train will be taken as nine-tenths of that sum. b. If the sum of the two vehicles' MLC is 60 or over, that sum must be taken as the combined MLC of the train.
Baggage and other pole-type trailers with a rated capacity of 1.5 tonnes or less will not receive a separate MLC but will be combined with their towing vehicles for MLC purposes.
The MLC of vehicles (or trailers or vehicle trains) of a total loaded mass of 3 tonnes or less will be optional.

Hybrid vehicles with a combination of axles and tracks assembled on the same chassis shall be considered as wheeled vehicles with large wheels, with the tyre ground contact length equal to the track length.

National or NATO MLC vehicle databases (detained by the national authorities in annex F) should include the following accessible data: a. Vehicle nationality, b. NATO code of vehicle, c. Name of vehicle, d. Type of vehicle (wheeled, tracked, hybrid), e. Total weight of vehicle, f. Number of axles , maximum axle weights and distances between axles if wheeled vehicle, g. Length of track if tracked vehicle, h. Ground contact lengths of tyres for large wheeled vehicles, i. Width of vehicle on ground, j. Vertical and lateral position of centre of gravity, k. Nominal MLC of vehicle, l. Rough/Uncorrected MLC, m. Method used to determine the vehicle's data (measured loaded axle data, maximum rated axle loads from manufacturer, rational estimate of payload, other), n. Span and controlling mechanism (bending or shear) corresponding to nominal MLC, o. If available, the table with the span-dependent MLC curves at the reference spans.
The databases must permit multi-criteria searches according to the criteria listed above.

Military Load Classification (MLC) of bridges is used to ensure safe passage across all types of bridges by wheeled and tracked military vehicles. The following parameters and methodologies are provided for guidance to establish this common load rating sys tem and are not intended to be detailed instructions for the design of bridges. The bridges and bridging equipment discussed in Sections 4.1 through 4.3 cover both civilian and military single and multi-span fixed bridging, as well as military floating bri dges, rafts, and ferries. Section 4.1 provides common rules that are applicable to the analytical load rating of all bridges regardless of type. Criteria that are specific to bridge type (civilian or military) are covered in Sections 4.2 and 4.3 . Because e ach country may prefer to develop their own specific procedures for classification, no specific methodologies are mandated.
However, in order to ensure a consistent level of safety, any methodology should adhere to the guidelines and minimum criteria outlined in Sections 4.1 through 4.3.

The criteria listed in Sections 4.1. through 4.3. are provided for MLCs under "Normal Crossing" conditions. A normal crossing allows unrestricted use of civilian bridges and normal accepted restrictions for military bridges, for all vehicles under standard convoy operation, operating at or below the MLC defined by the parameters of this document. Only the rating associated with the normal crossing for a particular bridge may be permanently posted for that bridge. The target level of safety considered acceptable in the evaluation of bridges for military use under normal crossing conditions is comparable to the target level of safety considered acceptable for civilian routine traffic permit vehicles in civilian bridge design and evaluation standards.

Certain tactical or emergency situations, such as the need to cross higher military load classes or obtain longer spans, may require the use of a more controlled crossing criteria and/or the use of less stringent safety criteria. For these situations , a rating associated with "Caution Crossing" or " Risk Crossing" conditions may be determined if necessary. This document does not describe ratings under these crossing conditions, however, suggested criteria and conditions for caution and risk crossing conditions are provided in Annex H. T he decision to use these criteria should be made at appropriate command levels using due caution considering the degree of urgency and the level of safety acceptable to the mission or situation.
All bridges shall be rated for both wheeled and tracked vehicles (dual rating).
Vehicular loadings are defined by the hypothetical vehicles in Annex A.

Shear and moment loading effects for longitudinal beams are defined in Annex B. The most critical loads (global or local wheel or axle) induced by any of the hypothetical vehicle conditions (with impact factor) will be used in determining the bridge MLC.

For local load under wheeled vehicles, it would be considered that the maximum tyre ground pressure can be up to 1100 kN/m² (11.2 kg/cm²) with a footprint whose length results from the load and the width defined in Column 5 of Annex A.
The safety concept used for military bridge assessment should conform to the local regulations. If unknown, a prudent application of the safety approach of another country can be allowed.

The used safety concept should guarantee a target level of reliability, appropriate to the bridge type, the vehicle, and the mission. The target level of reliability should be sufficient but may be lower than for civilian purposes.
The used safety concept should reflect a high degree of confidence for the bridge under specific loading levels and frequency of crossings.

Under normal crossing co nditions, the traffic load factor should be comparable to the value for civilian design, but reduced to account for the adopted (lower) target level of reliability. A reasonable benchmark to civilian target levels of reliability in bridge evaluation of military vehicles would be that of safety factors used for routine traffic permit vehicles on bridges.

If they can be quantified, systematic differences in load effects between wheeled and tracked vehicles may be integrated into bridge evaluation where possib le, still maintaining the target level of reliability. This differentiation should be applied with due consideration to the safety implications for all bridge users and can only be considered provided the bridge and vehicle data are reliable.
As each country has its own procedure and safety concept, no specific method will be imposed through this document.

Dynamic effects (sometimes called "impact") must be taken into account when establishing the bridge MLC rating. Practically, the static load of the vehicles must be increased by an appropriate fraction called dynamic load allowance (DLA) or impact factor.

While specific rules for the application of the DLA are not given, evaluators should conform to the local (or their own national) standard of practice, as well as guidelines, while considering the vehicle types expected to use the bridge.
As the DLA on smooth surface varies with the crossing speed, the chosen values, compatible with standard being used, must be adapted to the target crossing velocity of military convoys.

If reliable and referenced load effects data show that the dynamic effects of tracked or wheeled vehicles are significantly different, application of different DLA for both vehicle's categories may be appropriate.

As damag ed carriageways or obstacles on the crossing path can significantly increase the DLA's, the chosen DLA's must be adapted to the state of the carriageway unless the smoothness of the carriageway is restored and the obstacles are removed from the crossing path.

Bridges shall be rated for vehicles of the appropriate classification in convoys with a minimum longitudinal 30.50 m spacing between ground contact points. It should be assumed that all the vehicles in the convoy are of the same max imum rated class. For bridges with critical spans longer than 30.50 m, the rating shall be established for the worstcase position of the convoy on the bridge.
For two-way traffic bridges, the minimum adjacent spacing between ground contact points of vehicles positioned side by side shall be 0.50 m.
For rafts and ferries, the convoy spacing criteria does not apply. The minimum adjacent spacing between ground contact points of two or more vehicles positioned side by side shall be 0.15 m.
The desirable minimum headroom for bridges is 4.50 m. Where a bridge has less headroom than this, the rating will not be reduced but the headroom will be marked in accordance with
Special crossing limitations like width, height, axle load limits, etc. should be posted according to Annex J.

When the nominal vehicle MLC exceeds the bridge MLC, personnel sufficiently qualified in bridge assessment may examine the suitability of the bridge to carry that specific vehicle by one of the following approaches: a. Span-Dependent MLC information. If the span-dependent MLC curve is available for the considered vehicle (printed or electronic file), the nominal vehicle MLC may be temporarily replaced by its span-dependent value. Appropriate safeguards and systems must be in place in order to ensure t hat appropriate span lengths are selected to represent the bridge. b. Go/No-Go Approach. The vehicle is assigned a "Go" or "No-Go" status for specific bridges based on the vehicle 's suitability to traverse the bridge under normal crossing conditions. The suitability of caution crossings for specific vehicles may also be indicated. It may be appropriate to use the temporary MLC or loading details of a vehicle, if the loading and payload for a specific mission or operation are known. This process is typically conducted using software and databases and is linked with geomatics, engineering and logistic control systems.

The ability to perform a complete engineering level bridge analysis will depend on many operational variables, such as user expertise and training level, time on site for detailed reconnaissance, access to the critical bridge components, confidence in host-nation design, and/or construction practices, etc.

Permanent MLCs of existing civilian bridges suited for posting (see Annex J) can be fixed by the bridge owner. Calculations fulfil the following requirements: • The MLC is based on a complete and reliable set of bridge data including strength properties based either on bridge drawings and documents certified by the bridge owner or collected by qualified personnel using accurate bridge inspection tools. • The calculations are made by qualified personnel using detailed bridge models including techniques for optimizing the longitudinal and lateral positioning of the military convoy(s). The calculations must fulfil the requirements in Sections 4.1, 4.2.2 and 4.2.3.
• The used bridge data must be periodically reviewed. Any substantial change of the values or the level of damage must imply a re-evaluation of the bridge load carrying capacity.

Civilian bridges may also be classified with other methodologies - based on incomplete sets of bridge data (quick bridge reconnaissance), less reliable data, assumed values or simplified bridge models - resulting in temporary MLCs. The extent of usage for temporary MLCs is a command decision. Temporary MLCs must be replaced by permanent MLCs as soon as practical. The engineering analyses used for development of these methodologies must be documented and adhere to the basic principles for permanent rating. Any required assumptions about unknown bridge dimensions or details must be conservative and provide minimum levels of reliability in accordance with Section 4.1.5.
The resulting MLCs - permanent or temporary - must be dated. All relevant information must be available for allied units on request.
Vehicular live loadings are described in clause 2.1.4.

MLC calculations must account for normal crossing of the vehicular loadings anywhere on the roadway surface , from curb to curb . The critical longitudinal and lateral position will be that which produces the greatest load effects for the structural components under consideration. In addition to the MLC axle load configurations in Columns 2 and 3, the maximum single axle loads in C olumn 4 of Annex A should also be considered for components that are more susceptible to short-span loadings, such as culverts, masonry arches, or the floor systems of long-span bridges (i.e., stringers and floor beams).

The dead load shall consist of the weight of all structural elements plus all ancillary components such as railings, utilities, etc. If the bridge will be utilized during times of heavy mud or snow, these loadings may also require consideration.

While various combinations of secondary loadi ngs (such as wind and seismic forces) and horizontal forces (such as braking or acceleration forces) are normally considered in bridge designs, they do not require consideration for military load classification of existing bridges unless one of these loadings will obviously be significant during crossing of maximum loads.

For civilian bridges, the superstructure is almost always the controlling feature in bridge classification. Because they must span large distances, superstructure eleme nts must be made as lightweight as possible (i.e., their designs must be optimised). This can be done effectively since superstructure loadings are normally predictable. Substructures for bridges, on the other hand, must be much more conservative (less efficient) in design to account for unpredictable loa dings (stream and ice flow, barge impact, etc.) and unknown soil conditions. The substructure need not be checked unless it appears to be significantly deteriorated, unstable due to scour or settlement, or improperly designed or constructed.

When the load carrying capacity is limited by the bridge deck or other sub component governed by single axle load , the bridge MLC may be taken equal to the load carrying capacity of the main girders with a posted restriction of the maximum axle weight corresponding to the deck MLC.

The quality of the resulting bridge MLCs does not only depend on the bridge model used but also on the quality of the available bridge data: inaccurate bridge data or assumptions will likely lead to incorrect bridge MLCs. Bridge assessment methodologies can be prioritized depending on the classification process beyond the methods.

Weight correlation method . This method is based on the conviction that the maximum bending moment available to traffic is closely correlated to the maximum bending moment due to the dead weight of the bridge. This method requires detailed geometrical bridge data for estimation of the dead weight. This method is not suited for calculation of permanent bridge MLCs.

Traffic correlation methods . In these methods, the longitudinal load effects (UBM and SF) due to the hypothetical vehicles are compared to those inferred from some knowledge about the traffic allowed on the bridge. To that purpose, the required bridge data is very limited: mainly the span length and the width of the carriageway. This method is not suited for calculation of permanent bridge MLCs. The required knowledge about the traffic can derive from: a. Bridge design load(s). If the year of construction and the class of the road carried by the bridge are known, the bridge load carrying capacity available for traffic can be estimated from the effects of the design load(s) as described in the national standards. This variant requires a good knowledge of the nation al standards and assumes that the bridge was well designed to these standards and has not had a substantial decrease in load carrying capacity since it was initially constructed. b. Posted w eight restriction on the bridge accesses . Posted weight restrictions on bridges are generally for unrestricted movement of civilian non-permit traffic and can be used to assess available live load capacity for traffic correlation methods. c. Observation of vehicles running over the bridge . Obviously, the load effects of vehicles transiting over a given bridge are a good indication for the bridge load carrying capacity available for traffic.
Practically, assumptions about the vehicle's characteristics , such as axle loads and spacings, are necessary because they generally cannot be measured in the field.

MLC analytical methods . The bridge load capacity is calculated using pertinent structural data applying methods derived from classical bridge engineer design - or rating techniques. Two variants can be distinguished: a. Reduced a nalytical methods. These methods rely on accessible external dimensions and may assume many aspects of bridge construction (material properties, reinforcement or prestressing details) and assess only the most critical aspects of bridge behaviour. These variants are not suited for calculation of permanent bridge MLCs. b. Detailed a nalytical methods. The bridge load capacity is calculated based upon detailed knowledge and consideration of all pertinent structural data. It is a method by which a permanent MLC may be determined. The assessment may be completed using assumptions that are consistent with professional structural engineering practice.

Structural engineering software . Bridges may be assessed by applying structural engineering software which is not specific ally intended to assess MLC. This may be the preferred method of rating bridges with a structure not easily assessed by other methods or when the bridge is damaged. This type of software is generally not suited for use in an operational theatre. Only very experienced users should apply such bridge assessment software.

Other kinds of rating . Other bridge assessment methodologies may also be considered provided they are conducted and documented to conform with all the requirements of the present standard, for instance, rating based on bridge load tests.

All methods are complementary to one another and are best applied based on the accuracy of any data assumed in their application. Depending on this accuracy, an MLC may be based on the method deemed most approp riate for the available information or a combined MLC based on the two methods. In general, the methods will be consistent with the approaches used for permanent classification as outlined in Sections 4.1 and 4.2.

Because bridge damage is s o highly variable, a strict standardization for detailed damage assessment is impossible. However, a generic rating procedure that roughly categorizes bridge damage in terms of extent and ultimate effect on vehicular load carrying capacity is given here in order to provide a rapid understanding of a bridge's condition and potential for use in a military operation. These ratings require significant engineering judgment and should only be determined by qualified personnel.

The table below gives an overview of the damage type and effect on MLC relating to each damage level rating level. Damag e Level Damage Type MLC Effect Green Superficial No immediate requirement for reduction in allowable MLC Amber One or more critical load-carrying members has damage or deterioration MLC should be recalculated Red Severe damage to one or more critical load-carrying members is widespread or exhibits potential for total span collapse Damage is beyond determination of reduced MLC

The same criteria as outlined in Sections 4.1 through 4.2 shall be utilised for the determination of MLC for damaged bridges. However, special consideration must be given to the damaged members and their effect on the MLC. Whereas these members may not have controlled the MLC of the bridge in its u ndamaged state, they may control it in the damaged state.

The classification of military modular or tactical fixed and floating bridges rafts and ferries is typically accomplished as part of a rigorous standard development process where the desired MLC is a design objective. Since safety factors are generally low and weight limits minimise overdesign, this process typically includes a detailed design and analysis process followed by a thorough test programme to verify that design requirements are achieved.

In addition to the vehicle loadings described in paragraph 4.1.3, the dead load of the structure as well as other prominent secondary live loads must be considered when establishing the rating. These loads may include mud, wind, snow, braking, and hydrodynamic forces. The selection of which of these or other loads are applicable and how to apply them depends on bridge type or use and the national codes used in design.

For new structures or structures already in service with known data, a permanent MLC is assigned to a bridge once it passes the normal in-service acceptance criteria for a country. This process will include calculations normally verified by load testing. For fixed bridges, the hypothetical vehicles with the corresponding shear and bending moment curves will be used in conjunction with standard analytical and test procedures of the country concerned to determine the allowable safe MLC of a particular bridge.

In some exceptional or urgent situations, it may be desirable or necessary to use military bridges supplied by private industry or to use bridges of a non-NATO country for which a permanent MLC has not been officially assigned by national authorities. These bridges may be given a temporary rating. This MLC will be given for use under specified conditions and only for the specific campaign or exercise provided data supporting this MLC can be obtained. Bridges supplied by private industry which are advertised by that company on the open world market with a standard NATO MLC may be assigned a temporary rating up to that level provided the company warrants the MLC and/or offers test and analytical data supporting this MLC to the satisfaction of the national auth orities. Bridges of non-NATO countries may be assigned a temporary MLC if sufficient intelligence data is available to identify the allowable load capacity of the equipment and a correlation between the data and a standard hypothetical load can be made. On ce the specific campaign or exercise has ended, or as time permits, the bridge may be given a permanent rating by taking it through the standard procedures to verify the MLC.
The following parameters are uniqu e to the military load classification of military floating bridges, rafts and ferries and should be used to establish MLCs for this equipment.
Floating structures may be either of a continuous or discrete flotation design.

Continuous flotation structures or continuous bridge structures on discrete floating elements resemble a beam on an elastic foundation and therefore cannot utilise the shear and bending moment curves of Annex C to determine their MLCs.

Discrete flotation structures in general consist of individual pontoons that support a bridge superstructure. The floating support and the bridge structure spanning the floats must be considered separately when determining the maximum allowable MLC.

For floating structures, the g eometric and weight measurements prescribed for each hypothetical vehicle MLC are used to describe a common standard load from both a strength and hydrostatic/hydrodynamic perspective.

section: 4.3.5.3 Determination of loads and safe limits
text: It should be noted that for a fl oating structure either stress or hydrostatic/hydrodynamic criteria could govern the allowable MLC; therefore, floating structures must be checked for both strength criteria (ability to withstand the load) and hydrostatic/hydrodynamic criteria (ability to remain stable and floating). The lowest of these MLCs must be used to establish the allowable safe MLC. In addition, floating structures must also consider loads applied by the hydrodynamic forces caused by current velocity or propulsion through the water, anchorage systems, and impacts from floating debris, and grounding.

As a reference datum, it is necessary to define a standard current speed (taken at the mid-stream surface of the water). For situations where this standard current speed is not applicable (bridge or raft was previously classified at another current speed or where the current speed for the specific operation is known not to exceed a lower value) the bridge or raft may be classified temporarily for these conditions. In this case the allowable current speed will be specifically signposted along with the bridge MLC for that site.

It should be noted that these criteria assume a water depth of 2.50 m or more under the bottom surface of the equipment being used when loaded to the cla ssified capacity. Where the depth is shallower , the load carrying capacity of the bridge or raft can be degraded. The standard current speeds for permanent MLCs are given below. A Caution Crossing allows, with similar level of reliability as Normal Crossing, to cross with heavier vehicles or with longer spans by adapting specific use conditions.

To control uncertainty in lateral load distribution to supporting elements and reduce dynamic effects in bridge crossings, the vehicles must be driven along the approximate centreline of the way. They are guided and their speed must not exceed 5 km/h. Bra king, accelerating, and changing gears should be minimized.
Regarding fixed bridges, vehicles are only allowed to cross one at a time on each independent structural span.

Regarding floating bridges, several vehicles are allowed to cross only with a distance between vehicles greater than the one established during the design and testing of the bridge. This value (which must never be lower than 30.5 m) will not appear on the bridge but in the technical documents put at the disposal of the engineer in charge of the bridge.

Regarding ferries and rafts, the vehicles must be loaded at low speed and guided. They are set up in order to respect the safety and buoyancy of the system. They are braked and chocked to prevent rolling. Otherwise, it is necessary to avoid any manoeuvres of the ferry or raft that would cause turbulence and abrupt changes of direction.

For analytical classifications at this crossing level, the same level of reliability required of paragraph 4.1.5 still apply, except that consideration of a reduction in dynamic load effects can be made.
In addition, any benefits of having single lane traffic on a bridge designed for two or more lanes should be included in the evaluation where possible.
A Risk Crossing allows trafficking with heavier vehicles or with longer spans or with higher current speeds than a Caution Crossing by allowing for a lower level of reliability in evaluation.

Regarding bridges, the vehicles cross one by one per span which is structurally independent. They must be driven along the approximate centreline of the way. They are guided and their speed must not exceed 5 km/h. Braking, accelerating and changing gears should be minimized.

Regarding ferries and rafts, the vehicles must be loaded at low speed and guided. They are set up in order to respect the safety and buoyancy of the system. They are braked and chocked to prevent rolling. Otherwise, it is necessary to avoid any manoeuvres of the ferry or raft that would cause turbulence and abrupt changes of direction.

For analytical classifications at this crossing level, use all of the same assumptions as for Caution Crossing, except the level of reliability discussed in paragraph 4.1.5 may be lowered to minimum acceptable values.

Note that lower levels of reliability (often implemented by decreasing safety factors) often mean that the probability of bridge failure is greatly increased and even if complete collapse of the structure does not occur, permanent damage to the structure may occur, which might render the structure unsuitable for future crossings. For floating equipment, the probability of sinking or capsizing is also greatly increased.

The aim of this Annex is to standardise the method of marking of the military load classification of bridges and rafts and the corresponding marking of vehicles.
Participating nations agree that the NATO Forces will use the system of marking contained in this latest version of AEP-3.12.1.5.

The method is a military method and is in no way intended to supersede existing civilian methods. Its implementation is compulsory on: a. The vehicles in service in the different forces except for the vehicles mentioned in paragraph J.6.6; b. Military constructed bridges, rafts and ferries during training and operations; c. All operationally essential bridges in a NATO Joint Operations Area.
In peace time, the marking of existing infrastructure bridges is at national discretion.
The standard load method on which the computation of the classification of bridges, rafts and vehicles is based, is described in the latest version of AEP-3.12.1.5.

Special arrangements will be made by theatre commanders when vehicles or bridges depart from the standards defined in the latest version of AEP -3.12.1.5 (vehicles of exceptional width, low overhead bridges, …).
